utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Today we start late because another trial overran its time, and I say for the record that that is also why we started late yesterday. Mr. Docherty. Yes, Mr. Docherty, to continue your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Before I begin, Your Honour, a member of the Prosecution team is joining us for the first time today, Ms. Anamaria Turlea, seated to Mr. Whiting's left. She's been working with us for some months and will be helping out in court this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's very nice of you to introduce her and we welcome her to the trial, if indeed a person is to be welcomed to a trial. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Soja, good afternoon, sir. When we broke for the evening yesterday we had been talking about you making a trip to the Pretis factory in Vogosca, meeting a Major Krsmanovic there, and I believe that you had testified that you had been informed that there was a desire to re-work the ignition system for the modified air bombs. Is what I've said so far as a summary of yesterday's testimony accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From a later conversation with Mr. Krsmanovic, he clearly said that he was opposed to the modification works. The solution that we devised was intended for the launcher of the Ilidza Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So with that correction, the Ilidza Brigade was pushing for a modification, Major Krsmanovic was not enthusiastic about a modification, to say the least, was my summary of yesterday's testimony accurate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not really for him to say whether it's accurate. The records will say that, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just remind him of the testimony and move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: The question that was pending when we broke yesterday was: What was it that occasioned the need for modifying the ignition system and who was it that told you about why the ignition system was going to need to be re-worked?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the conversation with Mr. Krsmanovic we learned what the requests with regard to this system were. From what he told us and from our subsequent analysis we decide what problems were occurring with this ignition system. I would like to note once again that for the reasons that he believed that installing electronic equipment would render the equipment unreliable, he was against it. However, the Ilidza Brigade initiated the idea of finding a better solution than the standard one that was used before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Were there problems with the ignition of the modified air bombs?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: By talking to Mr. Krsmanovic I concluded that there were certain problems occurring. These problems were related to -- as he described to us by giving us an example of the first launcher that they used to operate, and the major problem was the connection between the cables leading or bringing the electricity in order to activate the rocket engines. And other problems that occurred related to the need to prepare the ignition or the fuse and to launch the projectile. So basically that was what we were able to hear from Major Krsmanovic in relation to the problems that they were facing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And did you agree to do some work and try and fix these problems?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We started this job only later, because when we returned to Energoinvest and after the conversation with Major Krsmanovic, I was a bit skeptical. I realised that he was not in favour of any changes. However, I was told that the Ilidza Brigade requested us to do this job. And we started working on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And what did you do to try and fix the problems with the ignition systems on the modified aerial bombs?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I mentioned earlier, there could have been potentially a series of problems. The first thing was to armour the ignition system and then to launch the bomb. We decided to solve this problem by introducing a certain level of electronic components into the system. The problem of connecting the cables that Major Krsmanovic pointed out to us was solved by installing electrical connectors that could connect these cables in a very simple way. And after considering the problem, I realise that these cables that were used to be connected with the battery conducted electricity, and the potential problem with firing was solved by us by using truck batteries in order to carry out the launching. All in all, it boiled down to fitting certain electronic components, not to the existing solution, but designing a completely new solution consisting of certain electronic components.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: In connection with the work that you were doing, did you ever go to the site from which modified air bombs were being launched?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Did you ever see a modified aerial bomb out in the field rather than in the factory?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Approximately how many times did you see modified aerial bombs out in the field?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it happened on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Let's talk about the first time. Whereabouts was this modified aerial bomb that you saw out in the field; and approximately when was it that you saw it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire job that we did in this connection and in relation to the manufacturing of the launching system lasted from about the spring until early summer 1995. I cannot remember the exact dates, but sometime after the first bombs were launched from these launchers, the first problems occurred. Mr. Popovic, my colleague and I, went to a location in Osjek at the confluence of the Zujavina [phoen] and Bosna Rivers. There was a malfunctioning launcher there. We repaired this malfunction and we returned to Energoinvest.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And where is Osjek? Is it east, west, north, south of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's south-west, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And at the time, were you aware was Osjek under the control of the army of the Republika Srpska or under the control of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the control of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: After this, you said there was a second time that you saw an air bomb launcher out in the field. Can you tell us where was the launcher that you saw on the second occasion; and if you can, tell us approximately the date that you saw it.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I saw air bombs twice, but I saw the launcher more than once. I suppose that you meant to ask me about how many times I saw air bombs. The second time I saw it, I cannot remember the date, was in early summer of 1995. I think it was approximately at the time when there was fierce fighting around Sarajevo. The launcher was, roughly speaking, across Energoinvest at the beginning of the Kasindolska street under a fly-over.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And why were you out at that scene? Was it felt necessary that you should go out to this air bomb and launcher under the fly-over?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I myself didn't believe that it was necessary for me to go there. However, they came and fetched me and took me there. The reason was that there was malfunctioning in the electronic system as part of the firing system which happened on many occasions. This was a location where firing was to be done in the vicinity of Energoinvest, and I thought that this was a very important launching operation because I saw many people there, presumably present on the location to attend the launching. They called me to go there and to verify these problems and, if possible, to try and rectify them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Were you told anything about what the military wanted to do with this modified aerial bomb that was under the fly-over?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This bomb was used to fire at the cold storage facility in Stup. At least that was the idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And did you learn what was at the cold storage facility in Stup such that the military would want to launch a bomb against it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This cold storage facility was a building made of concrete. It was in a plane relatively close do Ilidza, and fire was opened frequently on Ilidza from that location, and when I say "fire," I mean small arms fire. It was clear when looking at this facility that it had been targeted many times and hit with various artillery hits. I presume that the idea was to try and destroy this cold storage facility which was a dominant feature in that part of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Did you work on the ignition system of this particular modified aerial bomb?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked on one ignition system for this particular launcher, because of which I had been called and which was supposed to launch the bomb against the cold storage facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And were your efforts to get the ignition system working successful?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That time it was absolutely impossible to fire from the system that existed on this launcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, you say it was impossible to fire from the system that existed on this launcher. Did you change that system in an effort to get this bomb to launch?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The launcher was at a place where it was spotted and it became a target of infantry fire. So it was practically left there at the place from which it was supposed to launch the bomb. Since there were other people there who were supposed to attend the launching, including Major Krsmanovic, he was very upset, and he demanded that the existing system that we made be removed and not used any longer. The men who operated the launcher complied with his request.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And at some later time, did you observe this aerial bomb being launched?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this unsuccessful launching, I went back to Energoinvest a few hundred metres away from the place where the launcher was. After some time, two men who operated the launcher came to us and asked us to make the cables which will enable them to carry out the launching with an auxiliary battery. And this launching indeed did happen in the early evening hours from that same location and by using this standard procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And the cables that you had made?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Were you there in the evening when the bomb was launched?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Did it hit the cold storage facility in Stup?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that place where I was, one couldn't see clearly what actually happened. Soon it became apparent that the bomb missed the cold storage facility. A little bit later on, I heard that it had exploded, roughly speaking, above the last Energoinvest building situated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And when it exploded up above the Energoinvest building, were there casualties?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were no fatalities. A number of people were injured, and as I heard, most of them were injured by pieces of glass, because -- and other debris, because most of the windows were blown away as a result of the explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: In addition to the two times that you have told us about that you went out into the field and saw a modified air bomb on its launcher, were you told of the locations of other modified aerial bombs around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I first went there to see Mr. Krsmanovic in Pretis, I think that he mentioned a launcher in Vogosca and, if I remember correctly, another one in Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And those --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about the Ilidza one, because I was involved in the making of the electronic components, and I heard stories that there was another launcher most probably deployed in Blazuj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: These various places that you have mentioned, Vogosca, Ilijas, Ilidza, Blazuj, which of the warring factions occupied those places, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any information that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had modified air bombs in its possession?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Soja, how long was it that you worked on this ignition problem for the modified aerial bombs? You said that it was in the early part of 1995, and I'm trying to ask now how many weeks, how many months did you work on it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're interested in the actual work that I did, which means analysing the problem in terms of electronics, it took about a couple of days. I don't think that we needed more than another couple of days to make a design on paper. The manufacturing itself lasted for another 10 or 15 days. But we also tried to find the proper material and boxes and connectors during that same period.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And these chunks of time that you described, two days to analyse the problem, two days to design a solution, 10 days to manufacture and so on, was that back to back, or were there gaps in there, or, put another way, was this a full time or part-time project?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were short periods. There were intervals between them. We didn't work continuously on this problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, that concludes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hello, Witness. I am a lawyer at the French bar and I am Defence counsel for Mr. Dragomir Milosevic, accused before this Chamber. I'm going to ask you a few questions, starting with two statements that you have made before the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You also made a statement for the centre of documentation of the police of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1996; do you remember that too?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like you to take a look at the screen before you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Just a point of clarification. I believe counsel asked the witness about two statements given to the Office of the Prosecutor. I show that there was one statement made to the Prosecutor's office and one to the police. Just want to get that clarified, if we could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are those the two statements you had in mind, Ms. Isailovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I did, in fact, say that. I said the same as Mr. Docherty, and the witness just confirmed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I am in fact talking about the declaration, the statement which is before us right now, and I'm now asking the witness to look at the screen and I'm asking him whether what he sees before him is in fact his own signature on the cover page of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now we're going to look at the statement more in depth. But before we do, I'd like us to be as -- specific. This statement was made before an agency for inquiry and documentation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That seems to be its name. And we're now going to see this document, 65 ter 3125. Now, do you recognise your name at the beginning of this transcript? This is what you can see before you on the screen, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And if we could now turn to page 4 of both versions, could you, Witness, tell me whether you recognise your signature on the B/C/S version, which is on the right-hand side of the screen?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Since this is -- these are statements made before the Bosnian authorities and Ministry of the Interior as well as a statement for the Office of the Prosecutor, we're going to start with the earlier one.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to page 1, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Even though it was an agency for investigation and documentation, this meeting took place within the framework of a criminal procedure; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to ask you a question regarding the circumstances in which this meeting took place, because we can see here that was under Article 151 of the criminal code. Were you told this at the time? In other words, did the Bosnian authorities or people with whom you had talked, did they tell you that this is all done according to a criminal procedure?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are various circumstances involved and it would take time for me to elaborate on the situation in which I gave this statement. Therefore, in order not to waste the time, perhaps you can ask some more specific questions so that I don't have to go from start to end.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to you answer my first question, which is: Did the police officers tell you, because this was all of course done within the framework of a criminal procedure, were you notified of the fact that you were questioned? That was my first question.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The policeman took me down to the police station, after which the AID agency officials came. They interviewed me at the police station. And later I was taken to the building of a court, where I confirmed the statement, and then in some offices of the MUP in Sarajevo I was investigated by -- I was questioned by two Tribunal investigators, the investigators of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly when you said that it was around those dates, the dates that we see on this document, the 27th of August, 1996 that all this took place? So the Tribunal and investigators from the ICTY interviewed you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I object to this line of questioning on multiple grounds, and I need to state them at this point. First of all, if counsel is implying that this witness had committed a crime and that is why he was under the investigation of the police, I respectfully put it that that is not proper impeachment of a witness. If the witness has in fact been convicted of a crime, that would be proper impeachment. But the fact that the police questioned someone in the course of their investigations should not be used to cast doubt on the character or the veracity of a witness. In addition, I put it that the questioning is irrelevant, and finally, Your Honour, the -- this relates back to why I rose a few minutes ago about whether counsel is referring to one or two ICTY statements. I double-checked the transcript and Ms. Isailovic said two statements that you gave before the Office of the Prosecutor. The one that I am aware of is dated 2004. It was eight years after the day in question. So if Ms. Isailovic has evidence that there were ICTY investigators present in 1996 when the witness was interviewed by the Bosnian authorities, I would respectfully request to know what that evidence is. And for all of those reason, Your Honour, I object to this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, yes. What do you have to say to the objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I was waiting for the interpretation. That's why I didn't answer right away. So of course I can give you my response. I thought that it would -- I would be able to organise my cross-examination in a useful way so that I can ensure a proper defence for my client. But what I said, we can check on the audio, we can check the audio. I said that the witness had given one statement to the ICTY investigators and another statement to the Bosnian authorities, and that is the statement that I'm interested in. And can you also, of course, check the transcript, but I put another question to the witness when the witness explained to us how he had been arrested or called to go for this interview, he is the one who mentioned the ICTY investigators. So it wasn't very clear in my mind, and this is why I wanted to specific this, to clarify this question and that's why I asked witness to tell us when he mentioned the investigators, did he -- was he talking about the events that took place around the 27th of August, 1996, because the other meeting with the ICTY investigators took place in 2004. So we cannot confuse one for another. That's why I put that question to the witness, and of course I could repeat the question, if you will. I wanted to know if -- when he was interviewed by Bosnian authorities if he also saw the investigators of the ICTY. That was my question, in fact, did he see them at the same time, basically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber will allow the Defence counsel to continue her questioning. If it reaches a stage where we consider it appropriate to advise the witness that he may object to any statement that might tend to incriminate him, then we will give the witness that warning. But at this stage we think the -- and rule that the Defence counsel may continue her line of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. But I would like to clarify one point: This line of questioning within the cross-examination was not to impeach the witness. I'm not trying to impeach the credibility of the witness. He is a very credible witness, but I wanted to find out -- or, rather, I wanted to prove my case. It is not the credibility of this witness that I am attacking at all. Furthermore-- or, rather I will continue, with your permission. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned what happened. A bit earlier you talked to us there was a meeting with the investigators of the ICTY. Maybe those were people from the Prosecutor's office. Did you think at the time -- or, rather, when you mentioned that there was an interview, was there another interview other than the one on the 24th of July, 2004?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can repeat what I have already stated concerning the statement. I gave that statement to the AID, that is, to the Bosnian police. They kept me in Sarajevo. I went there to see my pre-war friends, and as I was trying to back home I was brought in by some policemen. After that, the AID officials appeared and they interviewed me. I spent the night with a friend in Sarajevo, and I didn't go -- didn't dare go back home. The next day I was taken to the court building where I, once again, confirmed the contents of the statement. I was told that I provided that statement as a witness in a certain case, which wasn't particularly clear to me, and I cannot recall the name of the person involved. After that, on all occasions there was always someone from the AID. After that, the AID people took me to the ministry, I believe, to the Ministry of the Interior. Once there, I was introduced to two men whose names I no longer remember. I was told that these were The Hague investigators. As far as I remember, that statement, which I had given was at that moment translated to them into English. After a brief interview - it lasted, say, for an hour, that was the time needed to have that interpreted - they were released me and one of the AID men took me close to the former entity borderline, from where I proceeded home.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, did you sign the transcript of that meeting that you see on the screen before you after -- immediately right after, or did you sign this statement at another time, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right away.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Following the meeting that took place with these two officials from The Hague, you were told that these people were people from The Hague Tribunal, did you sign something?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I signed anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But you do remember that your statement was interpreted into English or translated into English?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was done orally. It was interpreted into English, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, following this meeting or this interview, as you call it, with the Bosnian authorities or the AID, as you call them, you did not see the Bosnian authorities until today?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And it was only in 2004 that you saw investigators from the OTP; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you've told AID officials, as you call them, AID being the agency for investigation and documentation, you told them the same thing as you told the investigators of the OTP; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But, Witness, today you said something that is different and it does not correspond to what you stated in your two statements, and you will maybe be able to explain why you've said something different. You've talked about the fact that you saw the launchers on two occasions. You said, rather, that you saw aerial bombs on those launchers. Do you remember saying this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you remember saying that? What's the answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you, Your Honour, I was not really paying attention.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Please, sir, answer verbally yes or no, because if you just nod, we won't be able to put it down in writing in the transcript. Sir, you have stated today that when you saw the bomb on the launcher in Osjek, it was near the Bosna River and another one I didn't really pay attention to what the other river was, but do you remember saying this today?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But you did not say that to the Bosnian authorities of the AID, and you also omitted to say this to the investigators of the OTP in 2004; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. What did I miss or omit? I said we were at that location and that we were sent there to repair the launcher. I don't remember when -- whether anyone had asked me about any bombs being on the launcher or not. That's the way I understood the question, whether at that moment there was a bomb on the launcher or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, my question was more directed toward the different statement of today. Today you said something different than what you've stated in your two statements, and we can maybe take the 65 ter document 3126 and we can compare the two, and I would like you, please, to go to page 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in English it would be page 4 as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Right after point 5, second paragraph, right after the number 5. You state here -- can you read this, sir? Aside from one statement that I described to the AID --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was shown a copy of a statement pertaining to an attempted launch at the refrigeration plant where the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina soldiers were and that I was never present when a bomb was launched. What is stated here is correct. Even if I saw a bomb on the launcher, that doesn't mean that I saw the actual firing.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So you were explaining this discrepancy in your statement with the way -- or the question was put to you. When you were put the question as to whether you saw the bomb on the launcher, your bomb is -- your answer is what you've stated today, rather, I saw it twice.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And you're asked the question, did you see the bomb being launched you say yes on one occasion when the bomb was launched on Hladivode on the refrigeration plant in Ilidza; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe I didn't understand you clearly today, then, but I thought that that launch had failed.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an unsuccessful launch, due to the electronic device that I had worked on. That particular component was taken out and replaced by cables, and using a battery and those cables without any electronic components, they managed to launch from the same position where the launcher had been standing.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And that evening you were there, you were there on the evening that the bomb was launched; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So then I must have misunderstood you, because I thought that today you said something else, and we can find it of course in the transcript. I have my notes, but I don't have the exact. Reference?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, I think you're going to put to the witness that he said something different today and say what that difference is, or please move on, you know?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. But I do have the intention of stating the differences. Maybe I'm misunderstood. I did say that I had the intention of talking about it, but because I am pressed by time in a certain way because the break is coming up, I cannot give the reference of the transcript. I only took personal notes and I can only rely on my personal notes. I did not take the reference of the transcript. This is why I wanted the witness to tell us and explain to us what he meant when he said the following things.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I was under the impression that Major Krsmanovic was angry with you and your colleague because the launch on the cold plant in Ilidza, in Stup had failed on that day. Is this what you've stated here today?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And then you came back to Energoinvest and you were asked to hand in the cables. Did you go back under the overpass for that launch, for the launch that was to take place that same evening?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were asked to make new cables that could make the standard procedure of launching possible by using a battery, and this is what was done at Energoinvest. Later, towards the evening, because at the time we who had work obligation and due to the fighting around the Sarajevo, had to sleep all time on the premises of Energoinvest company, we knew that the launching was going to take place. Apart from me, this launching was being observed by many people, because they had never seen this launching of a bomb before.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So, as you said, it was a launch that was to take place without any electronic devices.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And you were present when the launch took place when that aerial bomb was launched, in other words, but the bomb did not hit the refrigeration plant but the buildings surrounding Energoinvest; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was nearby, but I was not the only one. I don't know how close we were when the launching took place. And it is true that the bomb missed the cold storage facility, but it exploded somewhere above Energoinvest.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So, I can conclude, therefore, that what you have stated in 2004 and your statement of 1996 was not true, those two statements were not true. What is true is what you said today, is that in fact you had seen a launch that was successful, in brackets, because it was launched -- it was unsuccessful because it did not hit the target, but you did see the bomb take off from the launcher. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to counsel saying what you have stated in 2004 and what you have stated in 1996 is not true when counsel has not pointed to a single falsity in either of those statements, and consistently when challenged about those statements the witness has reaffirmed and has explained why it is that counsel is under a misapprehension about the import of those statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, if you are going to put to the witness that what he said in those two statements is not true, then you have to -- you have to lay the foundation for that. What are you alleging in those statements to be untrue? And put that squarely to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. What I said is slight more moderate than what Mr. Docherty stated. I said only that there was some discrepancies and I started to mention the discrepancies, and you can read it for yourself. The witness can also read his words in paragraph 2. There's no mention of a launch. There's an attempt of launch only. In B/C/S it's "pokusaj," which is attempt in English, and in French is "essai," which is also in English attempt. So if I rely on my linguistic knowledge, those two words, attempt and pokusaj, which means attempt, is not the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where is the second paragraph, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The paragraph 2 is right under paragraph 5 -- or right under number 5. You have the -- first you have number five and then after that, there's a second paragraph of this number 5 item.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But, Ms. Isailovic, you have not put these particular alleged discrepancies to the witness to have the witness comment on them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm terribly sorry, Mr. President, but I started by this, because it's possible to verify in the transcript of today and in the statements. This is why I started with paragraph 2. I even read in B/C/S, which says "izuzev jednog slucaja," and then I asked the witness whether he knew or whether he was able to explain this discrepancy, this difference, between what he is stating today and what he stated in his statements, in those two statements, and those two statements correspond to one another. Maybe we can leave it up to the witness to explain to us where do these differences come from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In the interest of clarity, I'm just going to put to the witness. Witness, in your statement to the OTP, to the Prosecutor, of the 24th of July, 2004, you said and I read: "With the exception of one incident, which I described in my statement given to AID, that involved an attempt to fire air bomb against a cold storage plant which was occupied by the soldiers of the army of ABH, I was never been present at the time of launching air bombs." Now counsel had put that today you said something differently. What is the explanation, if any, for the difference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I understand what the misunderstanding is. The crew of the launcher asked me to come to this failed launching, and I was present there while this failed launching took place. However, when a successful launch took place in the evening without electronic parts, and since this location from which the air bomb was launched was merely a few hundred metres away from Energoinvest where we used to spend all day long there and I was not the only one who knew that a launching was going to take place, we watched it. I cannot remember exactly how far I was. It was a long time ago, and in addition to that, the whole situation was for me stressful. And I wouldn't say that I was exactly at this or that place. But as I say, since this was a very close location, let's say, up to 150 metres, all of us were watching this launching. There were many people watching it. And this is, I believe, what has given rise to this misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, but can we agree on the fact that in fact you omitted to mention to the Bosnian authorities that you were present during launching and you also didn't mention that to investigators of the OTP. The only time you mentioned it is today. Is that right.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right. But you have to take into account the explanation that I just give you. The first time I was asked to attend it because of the problems, and later on I observed the launches, just like all the other people living in the houses nearby did, and this was also being watched by other people employed in Energoinvest.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now let me go back to your statement of today regardless these differences. From where you were, were you able to see the air bomb?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly. It was dusk, and I think one could see both the bomb and the launcher. The launcher was standing there all day long. It hadn't been moved.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And you were able to hear, I imagine, people from the Ilidza Brigade saying that the purpose of launching this bomb was to hit the cold storage which was supposed to be the nest of the Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was clear already during my presence in the course of this failed attempt at launch, and the launcher wasn't moved from that place. It could not have been pulled out because it was exposed to infantry fire. Therefore nothing changed with regard to the firing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can I just take the witness back to something that he said earlier in answer to the -- the question relating to the discrepancy. You said, if I remember correctly, that you cannot remember everything, and the whole situation was for you quite stressful. Would you wish to elaborate on that? Only if you wish to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the failed attempt at launch, as I said earlier, Mr. Krsmanovic was opposed to using electronic components. And when the bomb was launched, there were some people there wishing to see what effects it was going to produce. It was very noisy. People were shouting at me, demanding me to remove these parts, and after infantry fire was opened, the launcher was left in that position, and all of this, of course, affected me. And the whole day after this whole event, I was under severe stress. And that is why I would say with the reservation that some illogical aspects can be detected in my statement, because after so much time has elapsed, I'm unable to remember 100 percent exactly all the details, and I think one of the conducive factors to that was the stress that I was under at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you were under stress, and maybe the effects of stress were the ones that would justify the discrepancies in your statements given to AID and to the Bosnian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the issue here is merely interpretation of what I said. I was present during the failed launch in a sort of official way because I had been asked to come and be there as a person able -- capable of detecting what the problem was. And the second launching, I observed as an observer and not from a very close range, and I think that's the source of discrepancies. They never asked me whether I was watching the later launch, and probably due to the question asked of me and the way I responded to them, occasioned this misinterpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you said that the bomb was supposed to be launched and it was supposed to target the cold storage of Energoinvest. But at the same time, if I understood you correctly, you also stated that you went towards this factory to observe, to look at what was going on. Was it possible to go on the one hand where the bombs were being launched and to also go simultaneously to the place where the bombs were supposed fall? How can you explain this?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honour, I don't think that the witness ever stated that, and he can confirm this, of course, to us. The cold storage was in Stup, and he was working at Energoinvest. But if you wish, the witness could maybe confirm this to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, what's the answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Energoinvest location that we are talking about employed about 6.000 people before the war. So we are talking about a rather large area. We were at one end of this compound. At the other end was already the front line, and after that, towards Sarajevo in Stup under the control of the BH army was this cold storage facility. So the cold storage facility was not part of the Energoinvest complex. The bomb exploded on its way toward this storage in the vicinity of the buildings which are at the end of the compound, and I think that the distance is approximately over a kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But you've also stated that the launcher was taken or was under infantry fire coming from the territory under ABiH army. So in the morning, when there was an attempt to launch the bomb, there was this infantry fire on the launcher; is that right? These shots, this infantry fire, was it coming from the cold storage?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only assume that that was the case. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And in the evening, when you were present, you were not invited but you were nevertheless present during the launch, was there also infantry fire coming from the territory under the control of the ABiH army?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly. I don't think there was any fire around the launcher itself. But generally speaking there was shooting almost all the time. I cannot verify with any degree of certainty that there was fire at that particular moment. I'm talking about infantry fire targeting the launcher.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... If I understood you correctly there were a lot of people, all these people participated to this launch. They were people around looking at the launch. But the launch failed, is that right, it was a failed launch?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right. That is what happened during the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: No. Actually, I'm talking about the evening launch, the launch that was targeting the cold storage. And you told us that on that evening the bomb hit something else, it did not fall in the territory that was under the control of the army of the Republika Srpska. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: So you asked me two questions, the first about the people present there. I said that there were people attending the first failed attempt during day-time. During the second launch, I and a few colleagues of mine were watching this from a relatively close range. I don't know who was next to the launcher. It is true that the bomb exploded, although we couldn't see it well from where we were, but judging by the damage to the buildings, we concluded that it happened somewhere in the air towards the end of the Energoinvest compound where Ilidza begins, and that is in the direction of Stup.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: That is to say, on the territory under the control of the VRS; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So since you told us that you were present at Energoinvest, since you had your working obligation and you were there, you were permanently there, you never saw again another launch from that position; you never assisted another launch from that same position. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, what do you know regarding those air bombs that were launched from those launchers?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like you to be more specific. I don't know in what sense you mean, what I know about.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, my first question was to see if you can tell us anything about the bombs, not about the launcher but about the bombs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Again, open to the objection that it is vague. Ms. Isailovic, what about the bombs do you wish him to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I would like you to take a look at your statement and to the paragraph above item number 5 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you still on the same question or are you abandoning this question?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: On the same?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It's the same question, but I am -- I am going to rephrase this question upon your suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So, sir, I would like you to take a look at the paragraph above item number 5, and I would kindly ask you to read the portion above Desimir Popovic. So I would like to ask you to tell us what is it that you did not know about air bombs at the time? So, sir, is it right to say that you had never seen any document about air bombs?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I had never seen any documents relating to air bombs.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And you also did not know at the time where these air bombs came from?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You also did not know at the time where the motors, the reaction motors used for the launching of these air bombs, were installed?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I didn't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us - and of course you may tell us if you don't remember that you don't remember. But please tell us, if you know, when you talked about 105 and 155-kilo bombs, you say "krmaca"?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard about it. If your previous question concerned the weight of those bombs, I've heard of the figures of 105 and 220 rather than 155. I think it was 220 or 225 and 105, and I heard that the people usually referred to those bombs as krmaca or sows.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Who was calling them like this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, answer that and then we'll take the break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The name of the air bomb, krmaca, that is something that I heard at the very beginning of the war, when the first sorties were above Sarajevo. That's what I heard from people. I heard that people referred to those bombs as krmaca, and it was a popular term. People would say a krmaca landed, and if you heard anyone saying that, you would know that he meant an air bomb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, we were discussing the word "krmaca," which is used, according to you, for any air bomb; correct? Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be precise. Let us say it is correct. I -- although I don't understand what you mean by "any air bomb."

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me explain, then. On more than one occasion air bombs fell on -- on the surroundings of Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Was that then the word used, as you said, for the bombs that fell out of planes?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that it was around that time when I heard that people call certain air bombs krmacas. I cannot say anything more precise than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: At which time are you referring to? What time are you speaking of?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The beginning of the war, around that time, for the first time in my life, I heard the term "krmaca," referring to a type of air bomb.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But let's now talk about those air bombs that you saw on launchers. Who told you what those bombs were?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably heard about that for the first time at Pretis, and I think two bomb types were mentioned on that occasion, the 105 and 200 or 220-kilo type. I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You told us earlier that you never say any documents about these bombs, but did you know at the time what type of explosive was used inside them?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that then, and I don't know it now either.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: When you answered earlier the questions of the Prosecutor about modifications, about changes, to be entirely specific what sort of changes were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Instead of the type of launch using a special battery and cables going to the fuse and the rocket boosters, that is, in the case of the launcher used in the Ilidza Brigade, we put together an electronic component, an electronic system, making use of a truck battery. Instead of a regular trigger, we used the battery to initiate the process of starting the engines, the motors. There was a box with commands, with buttons to arm the fuse and to carry out the launch comprising several electronic components. That is simply put.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Please. Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you and your colleague, Mr. Popovic, never had anything to do with the bombs themselves?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, precisely, Witness. You were present at the launches of some of those bombs, failed or not. And I'm thinking more specifically of that launch which happened in the day-time in the direction of the cold storage in Stup. Can you now tell us, you were a guest there. You were -- or, rather, you were called upon, you were brought there to do something about the ignition systems. Now, can you tell us how the whole process went?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened often with the launcher to have -- that there were certain problems when launching and the launching site was close to Energoinvest, about 100 or 150 metres away. They asked me to go there to see what the problem is in case of an unsuccessful launch. And I suppose I was expected to fix the problem on the spot, but that is what I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Allow me to be a bit more specific. What we're talking about now, the time when you walked into this place, they intended for you to watch the launch. It was supposed to actually happen, right, it was supposed to be successful? Now what I'm interested in now, what I'm interested in now is what were the people supposed to be doing? Those people who were there to launch the bomb towards its target, what were they doing?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once I got there, the bomb had already been mounted on the truck. The rail used to launch the bomb from was put in a certain position, at a certain angle, as well as the mechanism and the truck itself. It was in a ready position, prepared to target the refrigeration plant. That was put in place before I came there. When I appeared, they connected the cables used to launch and then they had to be stretched and taken away from the truck to a safe place, and the bomb would be launched by using the command console. If you're interested in any more details, I believe there were three buttons on it. By depressing two, one could arm the fuse, and then depressing the third one and one of the previous two, the launch would be carried out. The electronic system was there to make it impossible for the bomb to be launched before arming the fuse. That's why they wanted to have the electronic system. That was its only role it had in practice.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And now, Witness, could you describe to me what the bomb looked like? What did it look like? As many details as possible, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bomb was green, oval-shaped. I don't know exactly how long. I would say one or one and a half metres. It had three rocket boosters attached. They resemble a tube. I wasn't able to see how they were connected to the bomb casing. I suppose they used screws. It was a regular bomb, an object rather difficult to describe. It was oval in shape, between one and one and a half metres long, and I don't know how many centimetres across.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But when you were in the military, when you were in the army in 1983, I believe you worked with -- you were in charge of a rocket launcher, multi-tube. I don't know if that's the right way to call it B/C/S visecjevni lanser raketa. Multiple-rocket launcher, in other words, is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. I think among other things, you had the JNA in mind when I served my military term in 1983. When there, I was tasked with three things, one of which was to carry out training within the artillery unit with a multiple-rocket launcher of 128-millimetre calibre.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And then what you saw in Kasindolska ulica under the fly-over, did that look anything like the system that you had seen when you were in the reserve, when you were in the military? I'm thinking of the rockets themselves.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, let's carry on with the actual launching process. What exactly happened during the ignition process?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. The ignition of what?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the ignition of the system that was supposed to launch the bomb.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the ignition of the rocket boosters?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the standpoint of us, the people who were supposed to work on that, some electricity had to go through a small resistor, and it is probable that due to an overcharge, to electricity being strong, the resistor was supposed to burn out and then that would be used to ignite the boosters. That was one of the principles in place.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Right, Witness, that was what ought to have happened, but what actually did happen is what interests me.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean why the boosters weren't turned on?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: No, Witness. What I want to know is what you saw. You were there as an eye-witness. I want to know what you saw happening.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: By pressing the buttons that were supposed to arm the fuse, one starts a reaction. Well, we can't actually see it because it concerns electricity. By pressing the buttons, the rocket boosters were supposed to be ignited. It, however, did not happen. They tried to do it several times without any effect. That's all we could see.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So the system, that is, the bomb as you saw it, and its boosters didn't move at all?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Was there a sound?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, how far were you standing? There was a lot of people there, right, and a lot of people who knew about this kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall exactly, but we were probably some 15 to 20 metres away on the side.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And if I understand you right, they tried to ignite it several times, pressing the button, right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the system would not ignite, there was no launch, in other words, then the reaction I had already mentioned happened. There was yelling and I was asked to take that down, to replace it, and approximately at that time the firing started.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But the bomb remained on the launcher. Now did the people try to take it off, off the launcher, or did they just leave it there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the people from the launching crew took the fuse off, and then they withdrew, leaving the bomb on the launcher.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, precisely where did they put the fuse? Where did they put the fuse of the -- of the bomb?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You said earlier, Witness, that one of the -- one of the people there pulled out the fuse from the bomb; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But where exactly on the bomb is the fuse?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fuse is at the top of the bomb, or let's put it this way, opposite from the rocket boosters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, I imagine all these technical details are relevant to your case? Please explain how.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, I'm going to explain. The witness is an eye-witness to the launching process. The fact is we have seen no one else, fortunately or unfortunately, no other witnesses to an actual launch of an air bomb. And because we, that is, the Chamber and myself and the Prosecutor were all less than technical experts, we don't know necessarily enough about it, so I'm trying to collect some technical details which may be useful later for a technical expertise and help us make comparisons with other expert reports that are already available. I notice some inconsistencies, but I'm not an expert and hence I can't use them much. I can't do my own expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But ultimately what are you trying to show, what are you trying to establish? This is what is not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm trying to demonstrate the nature of this object that the witness has seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But to what purpose? To what purpose? It's not the purpose of cross-examination. It must be something that is relevant to your case. This is not a class. I don't have any esoteric interest in the subject. I mean, it has to be something that is relevant to your case. We're not here just to gather facts and gather scientific data about the air bombs.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]. Well, actually, Your Honour, I think that the Chamber's purpose is to find out whether this was an air bomb at all. So what I'm trying to do is collect some technical information that's going to enable to us find out, with the means at our disposal, what exactly was on that launcher that day, which was seen by our witness, who obviously is not an expert either and has never had anything to do with air bombs. He told us himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So it part of -- part of your case is that what was launched is not -- was not an air bomb. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm trying to say is that obviously, it was a projectile of some sort, but I don't know what it was, and I'm trying to collect as much information as I can to compare what I've already got with what this eye-witness has -- has to tell. He's seen something, and for me, that something is very relevant. And I believe it's relevant for the Chamber which is supposed to establish the nature of the object in question with, of course, the technical analysis available, since we are not experts. We're specialists in law, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, suppose it turns out that what was launched was not an air bomb but some other projectile but that projectile caused the damage and led to the death and the injuries as set out in the Prosecution case, what would be the effect of that?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, part of the argument of the Prosecution is, one, that air bombs are weapons that can't discriminate, that are not precise, that can't target anything with any precision, that you can't select your target with a weapon like that. And also, that only the army of the BiH has this weapon which can't select its target. Now, for the Defence it is very important to find out whether, since we have a witness who can tell us that the target was in fact a military one and another question is what weapon was actually used, and that's what I'm trying to find out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Now I think you are saying something that is relevant. If you're going to cross-examine to show that the air bomb could in fact discriminate and was in fact precise and could target with precision, that's very relevant. But it does not appear to me that your line of questioning was leading to that. Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hesitate to make things even more complicated, but if that is the line that counsel is going to do down is that the air bomb could in fact be targeted, I'm going to object because --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Could in fact target, I'm going to object as beyond this witness's expertise and that there is no foundation for those questions. The witness before the break in answer to questions from Ms. Isailovic said that did he not know very much about air bombs; and on direct examination, he said he was brought in, he tried to fix the ignition systems, it didn't work, and he went back to Energoinvest. So absent foundation that the witness actually knows about the capacity of the air bomb to target, I'll object to that line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, I'm going to do this: I'm going to ask the witness a question in relation to the air bomb targeting the - what was it? - the cold storage factory because that is a question of fact, in my view. He can say whether the air bomb was set to target the cold storage factory and he can also say whether at that time the cold storage factory was in the hands of the ABiH army. So, Witness, I'm going ask you this: Can you say whether the air bomb was set to target the cold storage factory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And was it successful?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The bomb exploded earlier. It didn't fall down. It exploded in mid air, and I never found out, since I ceased all contact with these people operating the launcher, what happened, and the question is whether they themselves know what happened, why it exploded in mid air, whether it hit a tree or some other obstacle, whether there was malfunction. I don't know. But, at any rate, it missed the target. It exploded in the air.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And was the cold storage factory in the hands of the ABiH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Isailovic, I'm not going do allow any more questions concerning the scientific data in relation to the bombs. If you wish to direct questions about the target capacity of the bombs and the accuracy, then you can, provided you can establish a foundation such as to show that this witness is competent to give that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I shall simply ask one last question on this subject and go on to another subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely, if -- I want to know whether the witness felt certain that this was in fact an air bomb.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It looked like an air bomb. Everybody was saying that this was an air bomb, and I believe it was one.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is the last, last question. This was the first time you saw it, this particular occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I saw it twice on a launcher, and that was the second time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, I'm told you have seven minutes remaining. If you wish to use more time, then you know what you have to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I would, in fact, like to be given a bit more time. I have just a few more questions which pertain to the argument of the Defence. I think I'll probably need another ten minutes on top of the seven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps even less.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you actually come from the area of Ilidza; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the environs of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And you were a member of the VRS during this particular conflict. That's during the war, up to December 31st, 1994, right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And as of the constitution, the beginning of the Republika Srpska, you were a member of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not hear a response to the question put at lines 13 and 14, and I -- it appears from the transcript neither did the court reporter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you were asked, were you a member of the VRS during this particular conflict during the war up to December 31st, 1994. What's your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please ensure that you answer the questions. Don't just nod.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did hear the witness say "da" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... talking at once.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And that could be why. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, as of the creation of the VRS, you were a member of the Ilidza Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning I was a member of a unit, I don't know how it was called initially, we were organising defence of our own homes from someone. We posted sentries, and that was a sort of self-organisation. Later the Osjek battalion was set up in Osjek. At first it was part of the so-called Ilidza Brigade. Later on it became part of the so-called Igman Brigade, and from the Osjek battalion, I went to the Butile barracks, which was completely unrelated to either of the brigades.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, would you be able to confirm to me if the people who were members of this Osjek battalion, were those people citizens of Osjek?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You've stated a few moments ago that you were supposed to, at the onset, defend your houses?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to show you a map; it's 65 ter number 2829. And I would like you to show us Ilidza on that map.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like to ask the assistance of Madam Usher to give the witness the electronic pen. But in the meantime, if I'm not mistaken, you said -- when you were talking about the Ilidza Brigade, you called it the so-called Ilidza Brigade. I'm interested in that word "so-called." Does that mean anything to you or is it just a way of expressing yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if it was its official name. That's why I said so, the Ilidza-Igman Brigades were the names that we heard, we as ordinary soldiers. Whether this brigade had some military name like the 1st infantry so and so brigade, I don't know. That is why I used this term "so-called," but it was a commonly used terms, the Ilidza Brigade, the Igman Brigade, but I don't know whether those were their proper names. That's why I expressed myself the way I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, would you please look at your screen. You have before you a map. Are you able to orientate yourself on this map, and, if so, can you please show us where Ilidza is.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is Ilidza. Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know at the time what were the military units that were placed in front of you on the ABiH line or side?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean did I know their names? No, I didn't know their names.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: On this map, are you able to show me the direction from which the opposite side came from, when we talk about Ilidza? So could you please show us the direction with arrows, by drawing arrows on the map.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: The units of your battalion, did they align themselves along this red line?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when I was a member of this battalion, this red line looked completely different.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And you're talking about what period of time exactly?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the period while I was a member of the Osjek battalion. This is what you're asking me about.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And would you be able to show us this line, to draw the line from your memory of the way it was then?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult to that in this map. At the beginning, the whole Energoinvest complex belonged to the so-called BH army, if we want to be consistent in calling units their names. If this is Otis, and it was in the hands of the BH army at the beginning of the war as well, I cannot orientate myself well in this map, I cannot draw a line, but I know which locations were held by both armies.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But can we say that while you were involved in the army that there were permanent combats between the two warring parties?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was fighting, but I don't know what period you are referring to. I was in the army until the end of 1994. There was fighting, there were periods of tranquillity and peace and --
